findings.title: Use of queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown() requires Python 3.13+
findings.body: The code relies on `queue.ShutDown` (as an exception type) and `queue.Queue.shutdown()` (lines 132, 142, 238), both of which were only added to the stdlib `queue` module in Python 3.13. Sentry currently targets Python 3.11/3.12, so `queue.Queue` instances will not have a `shutdown()` method and `queue.ShutDown` will raise `AttributeError` when referenced. In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` (line 238) the `AttributeError` is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` and merely logged, meaning the queue is never actually shut down and the worker threads remain blocked forever on `work_queue.get()` since they have no timeout and no sentinel value to unblock them. This leaves daemon threads running indefinitely (though daemon threads won't block process exit, `join(timeout=5.0)` will always time out and `thread-queue-parallel` mode will never cleanly release workers), and the whole feature is effectively broken/untested on the Python version this repo runs.

findings.title: Worker threads block forever on queue.get() with no way to interrupt on unsupported Python versions
findings.body: `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` calls `self.work_queue.get()` with no timeout, relying entirely on `queue.ShutDown` being raised by `Queue.shutdown()` to break out of the loop during shutdown. Since this stdlib behavior doesn't exist before Python 3.13 (see above), setting `self.shutdown = True` has no effect on an already-blocked `.get()` call — the thread will never notice the shutdown flag unless a new item arrives. This means on consumer shutdown, worker threads can hang, and `strategy.close()`/`terminate()` won't actually stop in-flight work promptly, risking data loss or delayed shutdown during deploys.

findings.title: OffsetTracker.all_offsets dict grows unbounded for low-traffic partitions
findings.body: `get_committable_offsets()` iterates `self.all_offsets.keys()` but never removes a partition's entry when its offset set becomes empty (it is only pruned in `mark_committed`, which filters by offset value, not deleting the partition key entirely when offsets are completed without any commit happening, e.g. for FilteredPayload offsets added+completed immediately). Over the life of a long-running consumer process this results in slow unbounded growth of `all_offsets`/`outstanding`/`partition_locks` dictionaries, particularly for partitions that get reassigned/rebalanced repeatedly, since partition keys are never fully removed.

findings.title: Per-message metrics.gauge call on queue depth may add significant overhead
findings.body: `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` emits a `metrics.gauge` call for every processed item (line 150-156), tagged by identifier. For high-throughput queues (e.g. uptime results) this adds a statsd/metrics emission per message per worker, which may become a non-trivial source of overhead/metrics volume at scale, especially compared to the previous batch-based processing which could emit stats per batch rather than per item.

findings.title: num_queues defaults to max_workers but worker count semantics changed silently
findings.body: In `thread-queue-parallel` mode, `max_workers` (previously documented as thread pool size for `batched-parallel`) is reused to mean "number of fixed queues" (`num_queues=max_workers or 20`). Each queue spawns exactly one dedicated worker thread for its lifetime (in `FixedQueuePool.__init__`), so unlike `batched-parallel`'s ThreadPoolExecutor (which dynamically allocates threads bounded by max_workers), this always creates `num_queues` persistent threads regardless of actual load. This is a meaningful behavior change for the same CLI option across modes, worth documenting more clearly, especially since the click help text for `--max-workers` was only updated to "maximum amount of parallelism" without noting the always-on persistent threads per queue in this mode.
